sections.html:
Montana has adopted the Uniform Probate Code, which gives an estate two paths, informal and formal. Probate is the court-supervised cleanup after a death: collecting and looking after property, paying what is owed, and handing the remainder to those who inherit.

One person, the personal representative, carries it out; some call that role administrator or executor. Estate size and the presence of a valid will decide which path fits, and the Montana courts site has a questionnaire that suggests one.

Before an inherited house can be sold, somebody has to hold legal authority to sign the deed. In an informal appointment the clerk handles the application. Under MCA 72-3-225, the clerk may make the appointment effective after 120 hours of elapsed time from the death, and only after the findings required by 72-3-222.

StageRule and statute
Start the caseInformal or formal case, usually opened inside 3 years of death (72-3-122)
AppointmentClerk may act after 120 hours from death (72-3-225)
Creditor noticeNewspaper notice weekly for 3 weeks, then 4 months for claims (72-3-801)
Close the estateSworn statement no earlier than 6 months after appointment (72-3-1004)

As a general rule, a probate or appointment case cannot be opened once 3 years have gone by since the death (MCA 72-3-122). Exceptions exist, so an old inherited house is not automatically stuck.

A late informal appointment or formal proceeding is still possible when no one filed anything on the succession during those 3 years. The trade-off is narrow powers: the representative may hold estate assets only as far as needed to confirm title in the successors, and no claims except administration expenses can be brought against the estate. A will contest can be filed within the later of 12 months from the informal probate or 3 years from the death.

Moving early makes sense for a house left empty after a death. Without someone in authority it cannot be sold, yet property tax, insurance and wear keep adding up.

sections.h2: Who can sign the deed on an inherited house?
sections.html:
Under MCA 72-3-613, a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate property, land included, by public or private sale, unless the will or a court order says otherwise. The title company will want proof of that authority before closing.

Family can keep living in the house while the estate is open. Section 72-3-606 lets the representative leave real property with, or hand it to, the person presumed entitled to it, unless possession is needed to administer the estate. That same section makes the representative responsible for paying taxes and for reasonable steps to manage, protect and preserve estate assets.

  • Will in place: the executor it names applies for appointment and follows its terms.
  • No will: heirs under the intestacy statutes apply, and the court or clerk makes the appointment.
  • Joint tenant or recorded beneficiary deed: the house may skip probate entirely. A transfer on death deed form, tied to MCA 72-6-415, is linked from the courts site.
  • Joint tenancy or a life estate: Montana State University Extension publishes a guide to transferring such property without probate.

sections.h2: Creditor claims and how the estate closes
sections.html:
Once appointed, the representative runs a notice in a county newspaper, one issue a week for three weeks. It announces the appointment, gives an address, and warns creditors that claims presented later than 4 months after first publication are forever barred (MCA 72-3-801). Creditors the representative knows about may also get a mailed notice, which gives them the later of 4 months from publication or 30 days from the mailing.

A second cutoff sits in 72-3-803: claims not presented by the earlier of 1 year after death or the date in the notice are barred. Between the two rules, heirs and buyers can see when the debts settle.

Section 72-3-1004 covers closing by sworn statement. The representative files it no sooner than 6 months after the original appointment, and it must confirm the claims period is over, that claims, expenses and taxes are paid or arranged, and that distributees and known creditors received a copy. One year after the statement is filed, the appointment ends if no proceeding involving the representative is pending.

A sale does not have to wait for closing. Proceeds generally pass through the estate, so ask the attorney, or read the court file, to find out who gets the net money and when.

sections.h2: Cash sale of an inherited house
sections.html:
With a cash buyer the closing moves fast. Funds arrive without a mortgage lender, the personal representative signs the deed on the strength of the letters of appointment, and the title company files it with the county. Nothing needs fixing, emptying or staging beforehand.

Delays usually come from a will not yet admitted, heirs who disagree, a house left vacant in winter, or overdue taxes. Property tax does not pause for probate: one half falls due November 30, the other May 31, and paying late adds interest plus a 2% penalty (MCA 15-16-102).

Gather these before you take any offer:

  • A death certificate, any will, and the letters of appointment.
  • What the county treasurer shows as owed in tax.
  • Names and phone numbers for every heir, so each can sign off on the price.
  • Photos and a short repair list, so an offer matches how the house really looks.

With the paperwork in order, the buyer's title company matches the representative's authority to the deed, looks for recorded liens, and records the sale. No lender appraisal or loan approval is involved, and those are the steps that most often stall an estate sale.

Cash Home Buyers will write an offer on an inherited Montana house and fit it around the court's schedule. Treat this page as general information and not legal advice. For your own case, ask a probate attorney or the clerk of court.

The Montana courts point families to several places. Call the Court Help Program at (406) 841-2975 for free help with common civil legal issues, probate among them. The Legal Service Developer Program, part of the Department of Public Health and Human Services, answers at 1-800-332-2272. For low-income Montanans with urgent civil legal problems, Montana Legal Services Association staffs a HelpLine at 1-800-666-6899 on weekdays from 9:00 am to 1:00 pm. The State Bar of Montana has a lawyer referral service at (406) 449-6577.

The courts site also offers an affidavit of death, a small estate packet, and an affidavit for collection of personal property packet. For a small estate, one of those packets may save you a full court case.

faqs.q: How long do I have to start a probate in Montana?
faqs.a: Usually 3 years after the death (MCA 72-3-122). A late case is possible if nothing was filed in that time, though the representative's rights over estate assets are then limited.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Montana before probate is finished?
faqs.a: Yes, once a personal representative is appointed, unless the will or a court order restricts sales (MCA 72-3-613). Before that, nobody has clear authority to sign.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims against a Montana estate?
faqs.a: Four months from first publication of the notice, or 30 days from a mailed notice when that ends later. Section 72-3-803 also bars claims 1 year after death if that comes first.

faqs.q: Does the house have to stay with the personal representative during probate?
faqs.a: No. MCA 72-3-606 allows leaving it with the person presumed entitled to it, unless the representative needs possession to administer the estate.

faqs.q: When can a Montana personal representative close the estate?
faqs.a: With a verified statement filed no sooner than 6 months after the original appointment, once the claims period is over and the estate is administered (MCA 72-3-1004).
